claims.text: A stable protective oxide layer is the primary factor governing the high-temperature wear resistance of FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
Chromium-driven oxide formation is the key protection mechanism in FeNiCrCoCu coatings.
The initial material is a micron-scale FeNiCrCoCu coating on a conventional steel substrate.
The baseline coating has uniform composition and grain structure suitable for room-temperature applications.
Adding a minor reactive element such as Y will enhance oxide-layer adherence at elevated temperatures.
Chromium together with the reactive-element addition promotes formation of a continuous, adherent oxide film during sliding.
Reactive-element addition enhances formation of a dense chromium-based oxide layer during high-temperature sliding.
The dense chromium-based oxide layer reduces direct metal-to-metal contact.
The oxide layer hinders material removal and thereby lowers the overall wear rate.
Reactive-element-doped FeNiCrCoCu will have 20–30% lower wear volume than the undoped coating under otherwise identical conditions.
Reactive-element-doped FeNiCrCoCu will have a lower coefficient of friction than the undoped coating.
The proposed mechanism applies between 600 and 800 °C under moderate sliding loads in an oxidizing atmosphere.
Oxidation is the dominant wear mechanism within the stated temperature and loading boundary.
The optimum reactive-element concentration and composition for oxide adherence are not yet established.
